blocks.html: In two dimensions, position, velocity and force have a direction as well as a size. ModSim's Vector holds components (.x, .y) and knows its magnitude (.mag), angle (.angle, in radians) and unit vector (.hat(), length 1 in the same direction).

blocks.code:
v = Vector(3, 4)
print(v.mag)
print(v.hat())
print(v * 2 + Vector(1, 0))

blocks.title: launch velocity
blocks.prompt: Write launch_velocity(speed, angle_deg): a Vector with that magnitude at that angle above horizontal. Use pol2cart(theta, rho) (theta in radians; np.deg2rad converts).
blocks.tests:
v = launch_velocity(40, 45)
assert abs(v.x - 28.284) < 1e-3 and abs(v.y - 28.284) < 1e-3, f"40 m/s at 45 degrees: about (28.28, 28.28), got {v}"
assert abs(launch_velocity(10, 90).x) < 1e-9 and abs(launch_velocity(10, 90).y - 10) < 1e-9, "Straight up"

blocks.html: Drag has the same size as before, ½ρv²C_dA, but now it points opposite the velocity: direction −V.hat(). Gravity points down: Vector(0, −g).

blocks.title: drag_force
blocks.prompt: Write drag_force(V, system) returning a Vector: magnitude rho * |V|**2 C_d area / 2, direction opposite V.
blocks.tests:
s = System(rho=1.2, C_d=0.33, area=pi * 0.0365**2)
f = drag_force(Vector(30, 0), s)
assert f.x < 0 and abs(f.y) < 1e-12, "Moving right: drag points left"
assert abs(Vector(f).mag - 1.2 * 900 * 0.33 * pi * 0.0365**2 / 2) < 1e-9, "Magnitude is rho v^2 C_d A / 2"
blocks.solution:
def drag_force(V, system):
    rho, C_d, area = system.rho, system.C_d, system.area
    mag = rho * V.mag**2 * C_d * area / 2
    direction = -V.hat()
    return direction * mag

blocks.html: The book's baseball: mass 145 g, diameter 73 mm, C_d ≈ 0.33, hit at 40 m/s and 45° from 1 m above the ground. The state is two Vectors: position R and velocity V.

blocks.title: slope_func for the baseball
blocks.prompt: Write slope_func(state, t, system): unpack R, V = state; acceleration = gravity Vector(0, -system.g) plus drag_force(V, system) / system.mass. Return V, A. drag_force is defined.
blocks.setup:
def drag_force(V, system):
    return -V.hat() * (system.rho * V.mag**2 * system.C_d * system.area / 2)
blocks.tests:
s = System(rho=1.2, C_d=0.33, area=pi * 0.0365**2, mass=0.145, g=9.8)
dR, dV = slope_func(State(R=Vector(0, 1), V=Vector(0.0, 0.0)), 0, s)
assert dV.x == 0 and abs(dV.y + 9.8) < 1e-12, "At rest only gravity acts"
dR, dV = slope_func(State(R=Vector(0, 1), V=Vector(40.0, 0.0)), 0, s)
assert dV.x < 0 and dR.x == 40, "Flying right: drag slows it horizontally; dR/dt is the velocity"
blocks.show:
def event_func(state, t, system):
    R, V = state
    return R.y

for angle in [30, 45, 60]:
    system = System(init=State(R=Vector(0, 1), V=Vector(*pol2cart(np.deg2rad(angle), 40))),
                    rho=1.2, C_d=0.33, area=pi * 0.0365**2, mass=0.145, g=9.8, t_end=10)
    results, _ = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
    x, y = results.R.extract("x"), results.R.extract("y")
    plt.plot(x.values, y.values, label=f"{angle}°: range {x.iloc[-1]:.0f} m")
plt.gca().set_aspect("equal"); decorate(xlabel="x (m)", ylabel="y (m)", title="Trajectories from your slope_func")
blocks.solution:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    R, V = state
    a_drag = drag_force(V, system) / system.mass
    A = Vector(0, -system.g) + a_drag
    return V, A

blocks.title: The 45° hit, with and without air

blocks.q: Air resistance cuts the 45° hit from about 164 m to about 100 m. Which is also true of the trajectory with drag?

opts.t: It's lopsided: the ball comes down more steeply than it went up, because drag has slowed its horizontal motion
It goes higher than without air

blocks.why: Without air the path is a symmetric parabola. Drag keeps removing horizontal speed, so the descent is steeper and shorter than the climb.

blocks.q: How do you write drag for 2-D motion with Vectors?
blocks.a:
• Magnitude ½ρ|V|²C_dA, same as 1-D.
  • Direction opposite to the velocity: multiply the magnitude by −V.hat().
  • Acceleration = gravity Vector(0, −g) + drag/mass; the slope function returns (V, A).

chapters.title: Optimization
chapters.tagline: The Manny Ramirez problem: best launch angle, and the slowest hit that clears the Green Monster
goals: Wrap a whole simulation in a function of one parameter
Use maximize to find the launch angle with the greatest range
Combine simulation, an event and root_bisect to find a minimum speed

blocks.html: Fenway Park in Boston has a famous left-field wall, the Green Monster: 11.3 m high, about 94.5 m from home plate. The book asks: what's the minimum speed a ball needs to clear it, if the batter picks the best angle? Two steps: find the best angle for a given speed, then the lowest speed that clears the wall.

From chapter 22: drag_force, slope_func and event_func are defined in this chapter's setup, along with make_system(params), which builds a System from a Params object. Use params.set(angle=60) to get a copy with one value changed.

blocks.code:
p2 = params.set(angle=60, speed=35)
print(params.angle, p2.angle, p2.speed)

sections.title: Range as a function of angle

blocks.title: range_func
blocks.prompt: Write the book's range_func(angle, params): make a system with that launch angle, run it until the ball lands, and return the final x position.
blocks.tests:
r45 = range_func(45, params)
assert abs(r45 - 99.3) < 0.5, f"At 45 degrees and 40 m/s: about 99 m, got {r45:.1f}"
assert range_func(30, params) < r45, "30 degrees is worse than 45 here"
assert params.angle == 45, "Don't change the original params"
blocks.show:
angles = linspace(20, 80, 25)
sweep = SweepSeries()
for a in angles:
    sweep[a] = range_func(a, params)
plot(sweep, "o-")
decorate(xlabel="Launch angle (degrees)", ylabel="Range (m)", title="Range vs angle, from your range_func")
blocks.solution:
def range_func(angle, params):
    params = params.set(angle=angle)
    system = make_system(params)
    results, details = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
    x_dist = get_last_value(results.R).x
    return x_dist

blocks.html: Sweeping works, but maximize(func, [low, high], *args) finds the best value precisely using a golden-section search: it keeps shrinking the bracket around the maximum.

blocks.code:
def range_func(angle, params):
    system = make_system(params.set(angle=angle))
    results, details = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
    return get_last_value(results.R).x

res = maximize(range_func, [0, 90], params)
print(f"best angle {res.x:.1f} degrees, range {res.fun:.1f} m")
blocks.title: Best angle at 40 m/s

blocks.q: Without air the best angle is exactly 45°. With drag the optimizer finds a smaller angle. Why does drag favour a flatter launch?

opts.t: A higher arc keeps the ball in the air longer, giving drag more time to slow it, so trading a little height for horizontal speed pays off
Gravity is weaker at lower angles

blocks.why: Drag punishes time in flight. A slightly flatter trajectory spends less time losing speed, so the optimum moves below 45°.

blocks.html: Now find the height of the ball when it reaches the wall. Use an event that fires when x reaches the wall.

blocks.title: height at the wall
blocks.prompt: Write height_at_wall(speed, params, wall_x=94.5): at the given speed and at the best angle for that speed (use maximize with range_func, which is defined), run until the ball reaches wall_x and return its height there. If the ball lands before the wall, return 0.
blocks.setup:
def range_func(angle, params):
    system = make_system(params.set(angle=angle))
    results, details = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
    return get_last_value(results.R).x
blocks.tests:
assert height_at_wall(30, params) == 0, "At 30 m/s the ball doesn't reach the wall"
h = height_at_wall(45, params)
assert 15 < h < 30, f"At 45 m/s the ball passes the wall well above it, got {h:.1f} m"
hints: Pass two events, [wall_event, event_func]: whichever happens first stops the run. Check whether the final x reached the wall.
blocks.solution:
def height_at_wall(speed, params, wall_x=94.5):
    p = params.set(speed=speed)
    best = maximize(range_func, [0, 90], p)
    system = make_system(p.set(angle=best.x))

    def wall_event(state, t, system):
        R, V = state
        return R.x - wall_x

    results, details = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=[wall_event, event_func])
    R = get_last_value(results.R)
    return R.y if R.x >= wall_x - 1e-6 else 0

blocks.code:
def range_func(angle, params):
    system = make_system(params.set(angle=angle))
    results, details = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
    return get_last_value(results.R).x

def height_at_wall(speed, params, wall_x=94.5):
    p = params.set(speed=speed)
    system = make_system(p.set(angle=maximize(range_func, [0, 90], p).x))
    def wall_event(state, t, system):
        R, V = state
        return R.x - wall_x
    results, _ = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=[wall_event, event_func])
    R = get_last_value(results.R)
    return R.y if R.x >= wall_x - 1e-6 else 0

def error_func(speed, params):
    return height_at_wall(speed, params) - 11.3      # the wall is 11.3 m high

res = root_bisect(error_func, [38, 45], params, xtol=0.01)
print(f"minimum speed to clear the Green Monster: about {res.root:.1f} m/s")
blocks.title: The minimum speed to clear the wall

blocks.q: Describe the two-level search the Manny Ramirez problem uses.
blocks.a:
• Inner: for a given speed, maximize searches over launch angle (each evaluation runs a full simulation) to find the best angle.
  • Outer: root_bisect searches over speed for the value where the ball's height at the wall, at its best angle, equals the wall's height.
  • Each level wraps a simulation in a function of one parameter, so standard optimizers and root finders can drive it.

chapters.title: Rotation
chapters.tagline: Angular position and velocity, and how long it takes to unroll a roll of toilet paper
goals: Use angle θ and angular velocity ω the way Part III used position and velocity
Relate rotation to the linear motion of the rim: v = r·ω
Model a roll whose radius shrinks as it unrolls, and stop with an event

sections.title: Rotation, the same way as motion

blocks.html: A spinning object has an angle θ (radians) and an angular velocity ω = dθ/dt (radians per second). A point at radius r on the rim moves at linear speed v = r·ω. One full turn is 2π radians.

blocks.code:
r, omega = 0.05, 10           # metres, radians per second
print(r * omega)               # rim speed in m/s
print(round(2 * pi / omega, 3)) # seconds per turn

blocks.html:
The book's example: a roll of toilet paper with core radius R_min = 2 cm, full radius R_max = 5.5 cm, and paper length L = 47 m. If you pull it so the roll turns at a constant ω = 10 rad/s, how long until it's empty?

As paper comes off, the radius shrinks, so each turn delivers less paper. Each turn removes a layer of thickness k·2π, where the book finds k from the geometry: the area of the paper's cross-section (π(R_max² − R_min²)) equals its length times its thickness, giving

k = (R_max² − R_min²) / (2L)

blocks.title: compute k
blocks.prompt: Write compute_k(R_min, R_max, L) from the formula above.
blocks.tests:
k = compute_k(0.02, 0.055, 47)
assert abs(k - 2.8e-5) < 1e-6, f"About 2.8e-5 m per radian, got {k:.3e}"
blocks.solution:
def compute_k(R_min, R_max, L):
    return (R_max**2 - R_min**2) / (2 * L)

sections.title: The state and the slope function

blocks.html:
State: θ (angle turned), y (paper unrolled, in metres), r (current radius). With constant ω:

  • dθ/dt = ω
  • dy/dt = r·ω (the rim speed)
  • dr/dt = −k·ω (the roll shrinks)

blocks.title: slope_func for unrolling
blocks.prompt: Write slope_func(state, t, system) returning (dθ/dt, dy/dt, dr/dt) as above. system has omega and k.
blocks.tests:
d = slope_func(State(theta=0.0, y=0.0, r=0.05), 0, System(omega=10, k=2.8e-5))
assert abs(d[0] - 10) < 1e-12 and abs(d[1] - 0.5) < 1e-12 and abs(d[2] + 2.8e-4) < 1e-12, f"Expected (10, 0.5, -0.00028), got {d}"
blocks.show:
k = compute_k(0.02, 0.055, 47) if "compute_k" in dir() else (0.055**2 - 0.02**2) / 94
system = System(init=State(theta=0.0, y=0.0, r=0.055), omega=10, k=k, L=47, t_end=200)
def event_func(state, t, system):
    theta, y, r = state
    return system.L - y
results, _ = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3))
for ax, col, lab in zip(axes, ["theta", "y", "r"], ["angle (rad)", "paper out (m)", "radius (m)"]):
    ax.plot(results.index, results[col]); ax.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax.set_title(lab)
print(f"Your model empties the roll in {get_last_label(results):.1f} s, after {get_last_value(results.theta) / (2 * pi):.0f} turns")
blocks.solution:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    theta, y, r = state
    omega, k = system.omega, system.k
    dydt = r * omega
    drdt = -k * omega
    return omega, dydt, drdt

blocks.code:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    theta, y, r = state
    return system.omega, r * system.omega, -system.k * system.omega

def event_func(state, t, system):
    theta, y, r = state
    return system.L - y          # zero when all the paper is out

k = (0.055**2 - 0.02**2) / (2 * 47)
system = System(init=State(theta=0.0, y=0.0, r=0.055), omega=10, k=k, L=47, t_end=200)
results, details = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func)
print(f"empty after {get_last_label(results):.1f} s; final radius {get_last_value(results.r) * 100:.2f} cm")
plot(results.r * 100, label="radius (cm)")
decorate(xlabel="Time (s)", ylabel="Radius (cm)")
blocks.title: Unroll until empty

blocks.q: The final radius comes out at about 2.0 cm, the core radius, even though we never told the model to stop there. Why is that a good sign?

opts.t: k was derived from R_min, R_max and L; unrolling exactly L metres should bring the radius back to R_min, so the match checks the model's consistency
The event stops at the core

blocks.why: The event stops when y = L. Landing on R_min at that moment confirms that the geometry (k) and the dynamics agree. Checks like this catch bugs.

blocks.q: How does the toilet paper model connect rotation to linear motion?
blocks.a:
• The rim moves at v = r·ω, so paper comes off at dy/dt = r·ω.
  • Each radian unrolled removes thickness k, so dr/dt = −k·ω with k = (R_max² − R_min²)/(2L).
  • With constant ω, θ grows steadily while the paper comes out more slowly as r shrinks; an event stops at y = L.

chapters.title: Torque
chapters.tagline: Newton's law for rotation, moment of inertia, and a teapot on a spinning turntable
goals: Use τ = I·α, the rotational version of F = m·a
Compute the moment of inertia of a disk and of a point mass
Simulate a turntable pushed and then slowed by friction, and estimate the friction from data

blocks.html:
A torque τ (force × lever arm, N·m) causes angular acceleration α:

τ = I·α

I is the moment of inertia, rotation's version of mass. It depends on how far the mass sits from the axis:

  • a solid disk of mass m, radius r: I = ½·m·r²
  • a small mass m at distance r: I = m·r²

blocks.code:
m_disk, r_disk = 7.0, 0.5
m_pot, r_pot = 0.3, 0.4
I_disk = 0.5 * m_disk * r_disk**2
I_pot = m_pot * r_pot**2
print(I_disk, round(I_pot, 3), round(I_disk + I_pot, 3))

blocks.q: Two disks have the same mass, but one has twice the radius. Compared with the smaller one, how much torque does it need for the same angular acceleration?
blocks.why: I = ½mr², so doubling r quadruples I, and τ = Iα needs four times the torque. Mass far from the axis is hard to spin.

blocks.html: The book's setup: a turntable (a disk, 7 kg, radius 0.5 m) with a teapot (0.3 kg) near the edge at 0.4 m. You push the edge with a force of 2 N for 0.5 s, then let go. Friction exerts a constant opposing torque until it stops.

blocks.title: slope_func for the turntable
blocks.prompt: Write slope_func(state, t, system) with state (theta, omega). For t < system.t_push the push adds torque system.force * system.radius. Friction torque system.tau_friction always opposes motion while omega > 0 (use 0 when it isn't moving). Return (omega, alpha) with alpha = net_torque / system.I.
blocks.tests:
s = System(force=2, radius=0.5, t_push=0.5, tau_friction=0.2, I=0.923)
d = slope_func(State(theta=0.0, omega=0.0), 0.1, s)
assert abs(d[1] - 1.0 / 0.923) < 1e-9, "At rest during the push: torque 2*0.5 = 1 N m, no friction yet"
d = slope_func(State(theta=1.0, omega=2.0), 1.0, s)
assert d[0] == 2.0 and abs(d[1] + 0.2 / 0.923) < 1e-9, "After the push: only friction, slowing it"
blocks.solution:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    theta, omega = state
    tau = system.force * system.radius if t < system.t_push else 0
    if omega > 0:
        tau -= system.tau_friction
    alpha = tau / system.I
    return omega, alpha

blocks.code:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    theta, omega = state
    tau = system.force * system.radius if t < system.t_push else 0
    if omega > 0:
        tau -= system.tau_friction
    return omega, tau / system.I

def event_func(state, t, system):
    theta, omega = state
    return omega if t > system.t_push else 1   # stop when it stops spinning

I = 0.5 * 7.0 * 0.5**2 + 0.3 * 0.4**2
system = System(init=State(theta=0.0, omega=0.0), force=2, radius=0.5, t_push=0.5,
                tau_friction=0.2, I=I, t_end=20)
results, _ = run_ode_solver(system, slope_func, events=event_func, max_step=0.01)
print(f"stops after {get_last_label(results):.2f} s, having turned {get_last_value(results.theta):.2f} rad")
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2))
ax1.plot(results.index, results.omega); ax1.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax1.set_ylabel("omega (rad/s)")
ax2.plot(results.index, results.theta); ax2.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax2.set_ylabel("theta (rad)")
blocks.title: Push, coast, stop

blocks.html: Suppose you watch the real turntable and it turns through 1.0 radian before stopping. Friction is unknown. Use a root finder: which friction torque makes the model turn exactly 1.0 rad?

blocks.title: Find the friction torque
blocks.prompt: Write total_angle(tau_friction) that runs the turntable model (setup above, slope_func and event_func defined, I too) and returns the final θ. Then the checks use root_bisect on total_angle(tau) - 1.0.
blocks.tests:
assert total_angle(0.4) < total_angle(0.2), "More friction, less turning"
res = root_bisect(lambda tau: total_angle(tau) - 1.0, [0.05, 0.5], xtol=1e-4)
assert abs(total_angle(res.root) - 1.0) < 0.02, "The root makes the model turn 1.0 rad"
assert 0.1 < res.root < 0.15, f"The friction torque should be about 0.12 N m, got {res.root:.3f}"

blocks.q: State Newton's second law for rotation and the two moment-of-inertia formulas used here.
blocks.a:
• τ = I·α: net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration.
  • Solid disk: I = ½mr². Point mass at distance r: I = mr². Moments of inertia add.
  • Simulate with state (θ, ω): dθ/dt = ω, dω/dt = τ/I.

chapters.title: Case studies
chapters.tagline: Bungee jumping: springs, drag, events and a root finder, all in one model
goals: Model a spring force that only acts when the cord is stretched (Hooke's law)
Combine gravity, drag and a spring in one slope function
Use events and root_bisect to design the cord for a "bungee dunk"
chapters.prelude:
from modsim import *

params = Params(y_attach=80, v_init=0, g=9.8, mass=75, area=1, rho=1.2,
                v_term=60, L=25, k=40, t_end=20)

blocks.html:
The book's final case study: a jumper leaps from a crane 80 m up, attached to a bungee cord 25 m long. The stunt is to dip into a cup of tea at the very bottom (a "bungee dunk"). What spring constant should the cord have so the jumper's lowest point is exactly at the ground?

Three forces act on the jumper:

  • gravity: m·g downward;
  • drag: from a terminal velocity of 60 m/s for a falling human, as in chapter 21;
  • the cord: nothing while slack; once the jumper has fallen more than L, it pulls up with Hooke's law, F = k·(stretch).

blocks.code:
y_attach, L, k = 80, 25, 40
for y in [70, 55, 50]:
    stretch = max(y_attach - y - L, 0)
    print(y, stretch, k * stretch)

blocks.title: spring_force
blocks.prompt: Write spring_force(y, system): the upward force from the cord when the jumper is at height y. The distance fallen is system.y_attach - y; the cord stretches by distance - system.L when that's positive, and the force is system.k * stretch. Return 0 when the cord is slack.
blocks.tests:
assert spring_force(60, params) == 0, "20 m below the attachment: the 25 m cord is slack"
assert spring_force(45, params) == 400, "35 m fallen: 10 m stretch x 40 N/m = 400 N"
assert spring_force(55, params) == 0, "Exactly at the cord's length: no force yet"

blocks.title: slope_func for the jumper
blocks.prompt: Write slope_func(state, t, system). State is (y, v). Use: drag acceleration a_drag = -system.C_d_term v abs(v) (it opposes the motion; C_d_term is precomputed for you as g / v_term²), gravity -g, and the spring's acceleration spring_force(y, system) / mass. Return (v, a). spring_force is defined.
blocks.tests:
s = System(params, C_d_term=9.8 / 60**2)
d = slope_func(State(y=80.0, v=0.0), 0, s)
assert d == (0.0, -9.8), "At the top, at rest: only gravity"
d = slope_func(State(y=45.0, v=0.0), 0, s)
assert abs(d[1] - (-9.8 + 400 / 75)) < 1e-9, "35 m down, momentarily stopped: gravity plus the cord"
d = slope_func(State(y=70.0, v=-60.0), 0, s)
assert abs(d[1]) < 1e-9, "Falling at terminal velocity with a slack cord: no acceleration"
blocks.solution:
def slope_func(state, t, system):
    y, v = state
    a_drag = -system.C_d_term * v * abs(v)
    a_spring = spring_force(y, system) / system.mass
    a = -system.g + a_drag + a_spring
    return v, a

blocks.title: One jump with k = 40 N/m
lowest point
blocks.prompt: From memory: lowest_point(k, params) builds a system with cord stiffness k, runs until the jumper starts coming back up (stop with an event on the velocity, after the first moment), and returns the minimum height. make_system, slope_func and spring_force are defined.
blocks.tests:
low40 = lowest_point(40, params)
assert -40 < low40 < 20, f"A sensible lowest point for k = 40, got {low40:.1f}"
assert lowest_point(80, params) > low40, "A stiffer cord stops the jumper higher up"
blocks.show:
res = root_bisect(lambda k: lowest_point(k, params), [20, 200])
print(f"For a perfect bungee dunk (lowest point at 0 m) the cord needs k = {res.root:.1f} N/m")
ks = linspace(20, 120, 11)
sweep = SweepSeries()
for k in ks:
    sweep[k] = lowest_point(k, params)
plot(sweep, "o-"); plt.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.8)
decorate(xlabel="Spring constant k (N/m)", ylabel="Lowest point (m)", title="Designing the cord with your lowest_point")

blocks.q: Why does the event for the lowest point need the condition t > 0.1?

blocks.q: Walk through the steps you'd take to model a new physical system with the ModSim toolkit, using the bungee jump as the example.
blocks.a:
• Choose state variables (height and velocity) and parameters (mass, cord length, k, terminal velocity), in State and Params/System objects.
  • Write a slope function from the forces (gravity, drag, spring) via Newton's second law.
  • Solve with run_ode_solver; use events to stop at meaningful moments (lowest point).
  • Wrap the run in a function of one parameter (k), then sweep it or use root_bisect / maximize to answer the design question.
  • Validate against reality where you can, and iterate.
